ranking.rationale: The Wish is a tiny one-piece crescent that tips from a fingertip. Pico Press exists for compact support-free motion toys whose single push, spin, roll, or wobble comes from geometry, balance, or gravity. A crescent rocker with bulbous horns is that craft exactly: one printed part, one obvious press, a gravity reset, no hardware.

Mira Fold is close on scale, support-free printing, and a hand-first invitation, but her bar is a two- or three-part tactile puzzle with a hidden reveal. This Wish is a one-piece rocker with no interlock or transformation to discover, so she would have to invent a puzzle the request does not ask for.

A circular-arc rocker can make stable equilibrium physically legible (COM below the center of curvature). Ivy would be the right Inventor if the Wish asked for a demonstrator of that phenomenon. It asks for a desk rocker you tip with a fingertip; Ivy also rejects desk ornaments that merely gesture at science.

Bob owns Wish-specific kinetic machines whose gears, cams, or linkages are the spectacle. A one-piece gravity rocker has motion, but no mechanism-as-spectacle. Bob's hard rejects include generic fidgets and decorative motion, which this object would become in his lane.
Tess Loop makes flat-print modular pattern families that tessellate, reverse, and nest. A single crescent rocker is not a piece vocabulary or a field of arrangements.
Eve needs a consented personal subject — a real dog, room, rig, or relationship — transformed into a cinematic little world. The Wish names a generic desk object and supplies no personal reference.
Leo invents original printable games with rules, opposing players, and seeded simulation. A fingertip rocker is not a game.
Alice personalizes a known tabletop classic while keeping its rules. There is no classic ruleset and no personal subject to portrait.
Abstract Boardgame Oracle invents combinatorial abstracts with a handful of piece types on a rich board. This Wish is not a game and has no board.
